newsitem.title: UK: No U-turn on Fids but UK Treasury in talks-Darling.
newsitem.headline: No U-turn on Fids but UK Treasury in talks-Darling.

text.p: The Treasury will not climb down from its proposal to abolish foreign income dividends (Fids) but is discussing with companies how to soften the blow, Alistair Darling, Chief Secretary to the Treasury, said on Thursday.

"There's no question of any U-turn," he told BBC radio when questioned about a report in the Financial Times that the Treasury was ready to climb down after an outcry from some of Britian's biggest businesses.
Fids, introduced in 1993 to preclude double taxation of dividends, allow companies to avoid paying British advanced corporation tax on distributed forign earnings that have already been taxed abroad.
Some big firms have said they might even consider moving offshore because of the proposed tax change.
"You do have to be careful about companies who say, 'if something happens, then we'll leave the country'. They tend not to do that," Darling said.

But he said fellow Treasury minister Geoffrey Robinson, the paymster general, had already told parliament last Friday that ministers were looking at the implications of the proposal because they wanted to encourage firms to stay and invest in Britain.
"He said that he was...entering into discussions with those concerned because we are anxious to achieve a situation where companies are not adversely affected," Darling said.
The FT reported that the Treasury had been examining ways of enabling companies with high foreign earnings to continue to pay Fids without creating a new tax loophole.
